Observation > Pattern > Tentative Hypothesis > Theory
Theory > Hypothesis > Observation > Confirmation

bullets.text: The capacity to do mental activities—thinking, reasoning, and problem solving

slides.notes:
Number Aptitude
Meaning: Ability to work quickly and accurately with numbers.
Example: An accountant calculating financial statements without errors.
Verbal Comprehension
Meaning: Ability to understand and interpret written or spoken words.
Example: A lawyer reading and understanding complex legal documents.
Perceptual Speed
Meaning: Ability to identify visual details quickly and accurately.
Example: A quality inspector spotting defects in a production line within seconds.
Inductive Reasoning
Meaning: Ability to identify patterns and relationships from specific information to make general conclusions.
Example: A detective linking clues to solve a crime.
Deductive Reasoning
Meaning: Ability to apply general rules to specific problems to reach a logical conclusion.
Example: A doctor diagnosing a patient based on known symptoms and medical principles.
Spatial Visualization
Meaning: Ability to imagine how objects look in space and how they can be arranged.
Example: An architect visualizing a building design before drawing it.
Memory
Meaning: Ability to recall past experiences, facts, and information accurately.
Example: A tour guide remembering historical facts about multiple monuments.
slides.visual_text: Heading Intellectual Ability, with a small diagram showing Ability splitting into Intellectual and physical. Definition: the capacity to do mental activities, thinking, reasoning and problem solving. A list of 7 dimensions: number aptitude, verbal comprehension, perceptual speed, inductive reasoning, deductive reasoning, spatial visualization, memory. A comparison titled Inductive Reasoning VS Deductive Reasoning: inductive uses specific examples to make a general rule, finding patterns or stereotypes; deductive takes a general rule and uses it to make a more specific example, drawing conclusions from previous known facts and definitions. Two flows: Observation to Pattern to Tentative Hypothesis to Theory (inductive); Theory to Hypothesis to Observation to Confirmation (deductive). Speaker notes give a meaning and a job example for each of the seven dimensions.

slides.title: Social intelligence
slides.text:
Social intelligence
the ability to understand and manage people and to act wisely in human relations.
the ability to perceive others’ intentions, and skill in following a sequence of events in social interaction.
Emotional intelligence
It refers to the ability to perceive, use, understand, and manage emotions.
It composed of four sets of skills: (1) managing emotions to attain specific goals, (2) understanding emotions, (3) using emotions to facilitate thinking, and (4) perceiving and interpreting emotions accurately in oneself and others (Mayer & Salovey, 1997)

slides.title: Cognitive Intelligence
slides.text:
Cognitive Intelligence
The ability to handle reasoning, solving problems, applying tricks, understanding complex ideas, learn quickly and learn from experience.
Cultural Intelligence
the ability to function effectively in a diverse context where the assumptions, values, and traditions of one's upbringing are not uniformly shared with those with whom one needs to work.
cultural intelligence is a specific form of social intelligence, and one that moves beyond understanding one's own culture and context to an ability to cross cultures and situations.

slides.title: Measuring Intelligences
slides.text:
Measuring Intelligences
Measuring intelligences other than cognitive intelligence has not proven to be easy.
Most common method: measuring a person's 'intelligence quotient' or IQ. Based on a series of tests which assess various types of abilities such a mathematical, spatial, verbal, logic and memory.
The Wechsler Adult lntelligence Scale (WAIS) is the most widely used IQ test for adults. There have been four different versions of the WAIS: WAIS (1955); WAIS-R (1981); WAIS-III (1997); WAIS-IV (2008)
So-called “smart people” (with high IQ)-don’t necessarily adapt well to everyday life, work well with others, or succeed when placed in leadership roles.

slides.title: Emotions & Emotional Intelligence
slides.text:
Emotions & Emotional Intelligence
Emotions are an affective state of consciousness in which joy, sorrow, fear, hate, love, surprise and anger are expressed.
Common features for all types of Emotions
Emotions are highly focused
Expression of emotions are universal.
Culture determines expression of feelings.
6 major categories of emotions are: Anger, Fear, joy, love, sadness and surprise.
Mood (it is understood as a feeling that is unfocused, and relatively mild in intensity).
